title: IP and MAC addressing
starter: A parcel needs a house number and a postcode to arrive. Suggest why a computer might need more than one kind of address too.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: MAC addresses
facts: Media Access Control address: a unique address given to every network interface card when it is made.
48 bits, written as 12 hexadecimal digits in pairs.
Used by switches to send frames to the right device on a LAN.
stations.challenge: Why does every NIC need a unique MAC address?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Media Access Control address: a unique address given to every network interface card when it is made.
Also credit: 48 bits, written as 12 hexadecimal digits in pairs.

questions.q: When is a MAC address given to a device?
questions.a: When its network interface card is made

stations.name: IP addresses
facts: Internet Protocol address: identifies a device on a network so data can be routed to it.
Given by the network, so it can change when a device moves to another network.
Used by routers to send packets across networks.
stations.challenge: Why can your phone's IP address change, but its MAC address stays the same?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Internet Protocol address: identifies a device on a network so data can be routed to it.
Also credit: Given by the network, so it can change when a device moves to another network.

questions.q: What is an IP address used for?
questions.a: Identifying a device so packets can be routed to it across networks

questions.q: Which device mainly uses IP addresses to forward data?

stations.name: IPv4
facts: 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots.
Part of the address identifies the network; the rest identifies the device (node).
There are about 4.3 billion possible addresses: not enough for every device today.
stations.challenge: Why can't an IPv4 number be bigger than 255?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots.
Also credit: Part of the address identifies the network; the rest identifies the device (node).

questions.q: Which is a valid IPv4 address?
How many bits are in an IPv4 address?

stations.name: IPv6
facts: 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons.
Created because IPv4 addresses were running out.
stations.challenge: State the reason we need IPv6.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons.
Also credit: Created because IPv4 addresses were running out.

questions.a: The world was running out of IPv4 addresses

questions.q: How many bits are in an IPv6 address?

stations.name: LAN or WAN addressing?
facts: Within a LAN, switches use MAC addresses to deliver frames.
Between networks, routers use IP addresses to route packets.
stations.challenge: Which address would a switch use, and which would a router use?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Within a LAN, switches use MAC addresses to deliver frames.
Also credit: Between networks, routers use IP addresses to route packets.

questions.q: Which address does a switch use to deliver a frame?
Which address stays with a device when it moves to a different network?

stations.name: Network and device parts
facts: In 192.168.1.20, the first part (192.168.1) identifies the network.
The last part (20) identifies the device, or node, on that network.
Devices on the same network share the network part.
stations.challenge: Two laptops are 192.168.1.20 and 192.168.1.35. Are they on the same network? How can you tell?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: In 192.168.1.20, the first part (192.168.1) identifies the network.
Also credit: The last part (20) identifies the device, or node, on that network.

questions.q: In the address 192.168.1.20, which part identifies the device?
Which address is on the same network as 192.168.1.20?

final.name: Final challenge: sort the mail

questions.q: Does each item describe a MAC, IPv4 or IPv6 address?
questions.a: 180.17.255.1 = IPv4; 2001:0DB8:AC10:FE01:0000:0000:0000:0000 = IPv6; 00-15-E9-2B-99-3C = MAC; 32 bits long = IPv4; 128 bits long = IPv6; 48 bits, set when the NIC is made = MAC; Four numbers from 0 to 255 = IPv4; Eight groups of hexadecimal separated by colons = IPv6; Used by switches within a LAN = MAC

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: State what a MAC address identifies.
points: Part of the address identifies the network; the rest identifies the device (node).
Media Access Control address: a unique address given to every network interface card when it is made.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

exam.q: Explain why IPv6 addresses were needed.
points: Created because IPv4 addresses were running out.
Within a LAN, switches use MAC addresses to deliver frames.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Describe two differences between an IPv4 address and an IPv6 address.
points: Media Access Control address: a unique address given to every network interface card when it is made.
Part of the address identifies the network; the rest identifies the device (node).
Between networks, routers use IP addresses to route packets.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

exam.q: Explain why a device keeps its MAC address but can be given a different IP address.
points: Media Access Control address: a unique address given to every network interface card when it is made.
Given by the network, so it can change when a device moves to another network.
Part of the address identifies the network; the rest identifies the device (node).
Used by switches to send frames to the right device on a LAN.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
